cells.tense: You can read what is fair about a thing while it is still crossing toward you.
cells.ask: Pick what something arriving has brought you — a person, a chance, a shift — and write one plain sentence about it. Set it where you'll pass it again. No deadline on reading it back.
cells.core:
Some things come toward you and you can tell what is fair about them before you've decided anything. That knowing sits quietly. You don't argue it into place; you let what's owed be obvious and you don't audit it. People hand you something half-formed and you still see which part of it rings honest.

There is something landing in your life now that will give you something once it settles — a person, a role, a change already underway. Before you sort what's fair about it, write one sentence about what it's bringing you. Not what you earned, not what it costs. Put it where you'll pass it again.

The pull will be to inspect it first. It doesn't have to be inspected to be real. A thing can arrive before you've ruled on it.
cells.sheetLine: You see what's fair before you've decided anything.
cells.verb: weighing what is fair as it arrives
cells.place: the threshold where what is coming first shows itself

cells.tense: You will have already judged what isn't here yet and found it short.
cells.act: give a concrete piece of help and finish it
cells.ask: Give someone near you help they can actually use — a ride, a meal, a call made for them — then finish it and stop. Don't tally what it took from you or what comes back.
cells.core:
Part of you starts measuring a thing before it has arrived. Whether it will be worth the trouble, whether it will ask more than it gives, who will owe what once it's over. You call this being prepared. The effect is a door held shut, so nothing can walk through and disappoint you. Fairness gets checked so hard the thing doesn't land as itself.

Strength in a situation means holding it without gripping. Someone near you is carrying something heavy. Give them help they can actually use — a ride, a meal, a call made for them — then finish it and stop.

The pull will be to make it even. Let it be uneven. Holding something well doesn't keep score.

cells.place: the threshold where what is coming first shows itself

cells.tense: The threshold was crossed while you were still back at the wall.
cells.act: walk the route with someone who is lost on it
cells.ask: Walk the whole route with someone who keeps circling a problem you already got out of. Start to finish, and stay with it until they're moving. Then go.
cells.core:
When something new arrives, part of you is already gone from the room. You don't feel much about whether it's fair; you feel a step removed, watching to see how it goes before you commit. What's entering gets met with distance, and that makes the present feel thin.

What pulls you back isn't force. It's being useful to someone else. Someone near you keeps circling a problem you already worked your way out of. Walk it with them — the whole route, start to finish — and stay with it until they're actually moving. Then go on with your day.

Passing a route on tends to remind you where you're standing. You don't have to shove yourself into the room. Move through it once with someone, and the room is where you already were.

cells.tense: You're sorting what's owed in this moment without noticing you're the one sorting.
cells.act: list the pulls on you and mark which are yours
cells.ask: Put down everything pulling at you lately — people, jobs, old loyalties. Beside the ones you actually chose, make one mark. No verdicts on the rest, and no clock on finishing it.
cells.core:
You have strong instincts about what's fair, and you act on them constantly, and you rarely count it as deciding. Someone says something and you already see what's right in it and you're halfway to acting — asked, you'd call it being sensible. That isn't modesty. It's your own hand on the wheel, filed under circumstance. The weighing moves so fast you don't see it happen.

Start below the weighing. Put down everything pulling at you lately — this person, this job, this expectation, this old loyalty, however many there are. Then make one small mark beside each pull you can trace back to a choice you made. No verdicts on the others. No plan to clear the pile.

Seeing which pulls are yours doesn't require settling them. A mark is already a first move.
